entries.title: Zelenskyy visits Norway amid Trump White House tensions
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy met with Norwegian and Finnish leaders in Oslo and held talks with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Trump is pressuring Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Zelenskyy visits Norway amid Trump White House tensions

October 20, 2026

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy met with Norwegian and Finnish leaders in Oslo and held talks with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Trump is pressuring Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Norway on Tuesday as Ukraine faces renewed tension in its relationship with US President Donald Trump and his administration.

Finland's Stubb: 'Today was a good day for peace'

During the visit, Zelenskyy met with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo, along with Trump envoy Steve Witkoff. The US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the meeting remotely.   

Store described the meeting involving the European and the US sides as "good and constructive" at a press conference.

"US and European teams have done substantive work on key issues together with Ukraine," Store said.

Stubb said, "Today was a good day for peace." The Finnish president said Witkoff intends to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders and discuss ideas from the Oslo meeting.

The Oslo meeting comes as Zelenskyy has accused the US of withholding intelligence from Ukraine in advance of Russian strikes and delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles.

Zelenskyy: Early intel warnings from partners on Russian strikes resume

Zelenskyy said he held a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier in the day and said Ukraine is now receiving early warnings from its partners ahead of Russian strikes.

"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said of the Russian-launched missiles while standing next to Finnish and Norwegian leaders.

There are also media reports that Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a meeting to possibly discuss Ukraine and other issues. 

"I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them," Zelenskyy said, but added that if Ukraine is discussed, it would be acceptable only if Ukrainians are at the negotiating table.

Trump ramps up attacks on Zelenskyy as US midterms loom

Earlier this month, Zelenskyy criticized a deal struck between the Trump administration and Russia to buy Russian diesel fuel. Oil and gas export revenues are vital for the Russian economy and war efforts in Ukraine. 

Trump has criticized Zelenskyy and blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for high diesel prices. Prices have increased dramatically since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to US attacks.    

Zelenskyy on Tuesday said he is supportive of Trump's suggestion to stop attacks on energy sites, with Russia also doing the same in regard to Ukraine as part of an "energy ceasefire." However, Zelenskyy said Russia is unwilling to stop its attacks on Ukraine.

At a recent European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy smiled at the suggestion that he is being made a scapegoat by Trump.

The US president is looking for someone else to blame for high domestic energy costs ahead of midterm congressional elections onb November 3. If the opposition Democrats take back control of the US House and Senate, it could constrain Trump's powers in his last two years in office.

In comments to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, Trump said he wants Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia and suggested Moscow has the upper hand.

Ukraine has been fighting off a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022. In the past, Trump has blamed Zelenskyy for the war and on Tuesday again said it was up to Kyiv to end the Russian invasion.

“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”

Trump said he also spoke with Putin about Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher detained in Russia accused of acting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces.

"I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Nigeria records its first Ebola case, in capital Abuja
entries.summary: Nigeria has reported its first known case of Ebola during Africa's latest outbreak originating in the DRC. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the patient was a woman who had recently flown to Abuja from Uganda.
entries.content:
October 20, 2026

Nigeria has reported its first known case of Ebola during Africa's latest outbreak originating in the DRC. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the patient was a woman who had recently flown to Abuja from Uganda.

Nigeria's Health Ministry on Tuesday confirmed that the country had recorded its first known case of Ebola in the current outbreak. A woman who recently arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. 

The outbreak is thought to have started in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, not far from the Ugandan border, with Uganda the second country to record infections. It also recently spread to Kenya in limited numbers, with nine known cases recorded this month.

The overwhelming majority of known cases, however, remain confined to the DRC, particularly its eastern provinces.

What do we know about the Nigerian case of Ebola?

Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said that the patient was a woman who had "recently arrived on an international flight from Uganda."

She first began to exhibit symptoms on October 7, and was admitted to a private Abuja hospital on October 11, before being tested and diagnosed with Ebola. He said authorities had already begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient.

"We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all contacts the individual may have had," he said.

Nigeria's Center for Disease Control said two weeks ago that it was stepping up surveillance after the first recorded cases in Kenya, saying it was improving the country's preparedness for a possible outbreak.

"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of healthcare workers," the agency said.

Nigeria created an Ebola task force in June.

"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."

Over 9,000 cases in current outbreak, the fastest-growing on record

While Ebola does not spread as readily as highly contagious viruses like the flu or COVID, it is considerably more dangerous to those who do contract it.

The current outbreak, involving a lesser-known strain, the Bundibugyo Ebolavirus, has led to more than 9,000 confirmed cases and more than 4,300 deaths, a fatality rate of almost 50%.

Almost all the cases and deaths are confined to the DRC, even as more countries become involved. The first patient in Kenya died, and authorities believe the other eight known cases are all part of a cluster beginning with him. They say there's no sign of a spread beyond his contacts.

Uganda, which borders the Ituri province outbreak epicenter in DRC, reported 20 cases and two deaths quite much earlier this year. It was then declared Ebola-free in late August by the World Health Organization after reaching 42 days since a confirmed case. Tuesday's case in Nigeria could potentially put this status back into question, given the Health Ministry's comments on the patient's travel history.

This year's outbreak is already the second-largest on record and by far the fastest-spreading — although modestly improved testing and diagnostic capacity may also contribute to the higher numbers.

The West African Ebola epidemic of 2014-16 led to around 11,300 deaths from around 28,500 cases — but that was over a span of around 30 months. This outbreak was first declared in May of this year, although researchers believe it likely began in small numbers of cases several months earlier.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Lebanon faces uncertainty as UNIFIL mandate nears end
entries.summary: As UN peacekeeping forces prepare to withdraw from Lebanon, Israel remains present and Hezbollah is still armed. A new EU support mission aims to strengthen Lebanon's army, but will not replace UN peacekeepers.
entries.content:
Lebanon

Lebanon faces uncertainty as UNIFIL mandate nears end

October 20, 2026

As UN peacekeeping forces prepare to withdraw from Lebanon, Israel remains present and Hezbollah is still armed. A new EU support mission aims to strengthen Lebanon's army, but will not replace UN peacekeepers.

As the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, nears its end, uncertainty over the future of southern Lebanon is growing. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has warned of the need to "avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it."

The Lebanese government has also been pushing for a last-minute extension of UNIFIL's mandate, but so far without success. It is most likely that the 7,565 peacekeepers from 46 countries will begin withdrawing from the UN-patrolled so-called Blue Line zone on December 31, 2026. 

The Blue Line, which stretches for 120 kilometers (75 miles), is a UN-identified line of withdrawal between Israel and Lebanon, not an internationally agreed border. It was established in 2000. However, as early as in 1978, multinational UNIFIL troops were deployed to this region to monitor the area after Israel invaded Lebanon in response to attacks by Palestinian armed groups.

After the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war, the mandate was expanded to support the Lebanese army in implementing UN Security Council Resolution 1701. The resolution calls for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River to be free of armed personnel, assets and weapons other than those belonging to the Lebanese government and UNIFIL. It also calls for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.

However, following cross-border attacks by Hezbollah in October 2023 and the ensuing war in 2024, Israel has been occupying large swaths of Lebanese territory in a self-declared security zone called the Yellow Line, which is located north of the Blue Line.

Of the more than 1.2 million people displaced in Lebanon during the renewed conflict in 2026, around 329,000 remained internally displaced as of September 29, according to the International Organization for Migration. Israel has also caused extensive destruction to homes and key infrastructure in southern Lebanon, saying it needs to protect its citizens in northern Israel from attacks launched from the area.

Hezbollah — which is designated as a terrorist organization by several countries, including the United States and Germany, while the European Union designates its armed wing as a terrorist organization — continues to reject disarmament, citing the need to defend itself for as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.

Hezbollah is also closely linked to Iran, and in case of renewed conflict between Iran and Israel, it's likely that Hezbollah would open a second front in Israel's north in support of Iran.

"The situation in southern Lebanon remains tense," Kandice Ardiel, UNIFIL's spokesperson, told DW. "We are seeing continued Israeli military operations, including overflights of Lebanese airspace by jets, helicopters and drones, airstrikes, artillery strikes and mortar fire." 

"Until our mandate ends on December 31, we continue to monitor and report what is happening, and we are liaising between the parties on a daily basis to ensure safe movements of civilians, humanitarian aid, and peacekeeping patrols," she said, adding that the drawdown and withdrawal would then take place in stages.

The end of the mandate also means the end of the mission for thousands of UNIFIL troops in southern Lebanon. "People have built careers, friendships, skills and a sense of purpose together," Ardiel said. "Endings are never easy, especially when there is a sense that the work we do is still needed."

Beirut's lack of authority, money compounds disarmament dilemma

The upcoming withdrawal of UNIFIL also highlights two major dilemmas for Lebanon's government.

"Beirut is concerned that violations of any agreements, whether on the Israeli or the Hezbollah side, can't be tracked in the absence of an international military force," Paul Shaya, a Washington-based Middle East researcher and adjunct professor at George Washington University, told DW.

Furthermore, after years of political deadlock, the COVID-19 pandemic, soaring inflation and economic crises, the Beirut port blast in 2020 and the destruction caused by the 2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah, Lebanon's economic lifeline depends on international funding. However, a large share of the much-needed investment from the United States and Gulf states is tied to Hezbollah's disarmament.

"Ultimately, it is going to be dependent on President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam to secure sufficient funding and resources to support the Lebanese military," said Shaya.

Until that happens, Aoun and Salam have very limited options for disarming Hezbollah, said David Wood, Lebanon researcher at the International Crisis Group. "They have opened direct talks with Israel to bring about an end to the disastrous conflict, but that process includes neither Hezbollah nor its backer Iran — both of which oppose the group's disarmament," he said.

In Wood's view, Beirut has few bargaining chips in negotiations with Israel because it has been unable to secure Hezbollah's compliance. He is also worried that Lebanon's leaders have little leverage to force Hezbollah to surrender its weapons, as this could trigger a deadly domestic conflict in the country. In the past, Hezbollah has openly warned that trying to seize its weapons by force would lead to war.

Despite Israel's destruction of many Hezbollah tunnels and weapons-storage facilities in Hezbollah-dominated areas in southern Lebanon and parts of Beirut, the limitation or disruption of supply routes due to the wider Iran war, as well as the fall of their ally, Syrian President Bashar Assad, observers say Hezbollah remains better equipped than the Lebanese armed forces.

Could the new EU mission replace UNIFIL in Lebanon?

On October 12, European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, with an initial three-year mandate.

"It has a civilian and military pillar," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, adding that "this is highly welcomed by the local authorities."

According to the European Council, the mission is to contribute to peace and security in Lebanon by strengthening the capabilities of the Lebanese armed forces and internal security forces, including in border security in accordance with the UN Security Council Resolution 1701.

However, the mission is not intended to replace UNIFIL. Rather than deploying peacekeepers to patrol southern Lebanon, it is set to initially operate north of the Litani River.

Several existing UNIFIL contributors, including Italy, France, Spain, Ireland, Germany, Austria, Finland and Poland, already expressed interest in contributing personnel and resources to the new EUSM Lebanon mission.

For the government in Beirut, this is a positive signal, noted Shaya. He added that Lebanese society also strongly supports the Lebanese military, "which many see as the only institution in the country that can uphold Lebanon's sovereignty and represent the entire country."

entries.title: Sudan drone strike kills around 150 in Abyei market
entries.summary: A drone strike hit a market in the Abyei border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan and killed dozens. The drone caused a large fire when it hit a fuel depot. South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military.
entries.content:
Sudan

Sudan drone strike kills around 150 in Abyei market

October 20, 2026

A drone strike hit a market in the Abyei border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan and killed dozens. The drone caused a large fire when it hit a fuel depot. South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military.

A drone strike in a busy market in the disputed region of Abyei has killed more than 150 people, according to local officials. 

South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military for the attack, without providing evidence, amid the long-running civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which is reportedly active in the Abyei area.

The special UN mission in Abyei warned in May that the RSF's presence in the resource-rich region had put residents in additional danger, and risked intensifying the older territorial dispute between Sudan and the world's newest sovereign state, South Sudan. 

What do we know about the drone strike?

According to local authorities, the attack hit the busy Amiet Market at around midday on Monday.

Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker information minister in Abyei, told Reuters news agency on Tuesday that the death toll had more than doubled, reaching at least 153 compared to a stated figure of 73 the previous day.

He said that Sudan's military was responsible for the attack but did not provide evidence. Akol Ngor said around 8,000 people had been displaced by the bombing.

South Sudan's Foreign Ministry also blamed the Sudanese army and said the drone struck multiple locations around the busy market.

One of these, judging by witness accounts, was a fuel depot — and this led to a large fire that proved difficult to bring under control overnight and was still ablaze on Tuesday.

South Sudan said it had summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to "refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property."

Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders, said that its staff was treating some 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek hospital.

"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted," said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF's medical activities manager at the hospital.

What's the backstory of Sudan, South Sudan and Abyei?

The oil-rich Abyei region's status was not resolved by the 2005 peace agreement that broadly ended decades of civil war in Sudan.

It was also not settled in 2011 when South Sudan became an independent country.

A referendum was planned but never materialized, stalling over disputes on who should be allowed to vote. This left Abyei in a state of limbo, jointly administered and with an interim UN security force on site for 15 years.

The region's majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan.

Amiet Market, the site of the attack, is an important trading hub for both communities.

The unstable region has also experienced intercommunal violence in recent years between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities and is home to other armed militias.

How does this fit into Sudan's army's war with the RSF?

The April 2023 outbreak of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary — which has turned into a conflict with fairly entrenched battle lines, putting Sudan into a de facto state of partition — is increasing tension in the already-strained region.

Abyei borders South Kordofan state in Sudan, which has become a major center of fighting in the war.

Sudan's military alleges that the RSF is also operating out of Abyei. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) issued a similar statement in May.

Officials in Abyei and South Sudan dispute this, however.

Sudan's military and the RSF have both been using drones extensively in the conflict. 

"We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure — these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters in New York on Tuesday when asked about the attack.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: North Korean workers treated as 'slaves' at Russian drone factory, says new report
entries.summary: A new report reveals the plight of North Korean workers at a drone factory in Russia. It also raised concerns that Pyongyang could gain hands-on knowledge of advanced weapons systems through the workers it sends there.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korean workers treated as 'slaves' at Russian drone factory

October 20, 2026

A new report reveals the plight of North Korean workers at a drone factory in Russia. It also raised concerns that Pyongyang could gain hands-on knowledge of advanced weapons systems through the workers it sends there.

As many as 12,000 North Koreans working at a Russian drone factory are victims of "gross human rights abuses and human trafficking," according to a new report.

The figures were part of a joint report published on October 14 by the  Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the Dallas-based George W. Bush Institute. It analyzes how Russia, North Korea, China and Iran are involved in expanding unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) production at the Yelabuga plant in Tatarstan, and what each country stands to gain.

While Moscow gets access to more than 5,500 drones a month for its war against Ukraine, China benefits from being the main supplier of dual-use components, including batteries, internal electronics, engines and navigation systems. 

Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drones, which has helped Moscow produce upgraded domestic variants, known as Geran.

Meanwhile, North Korea is earning money by retaining as much as 90% of the wages of the laborers, the report stated.

"The geographical locations of these four countries… means that any kind of international interdiction is impossible," Dan Pinkston, a professor of international relations at the Seoul campus of Troy University, told DW.

Russia and North Korea defy UN resolutions

The joint report says Russia and North Korea are defying United Nations Security Council Resolution 2397, of December 2017, which requires any UN member state to send North Korean workers home within two years.

"The North Korean regime… is selling the labor of its citizens under a state-to-state arrangement, controlling whether they may leave and collecting most of their wages," it said. This, according to the report, "is the definition of forced labor."

Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist with the Worldwide Coalition to Stop Genocide in North Korea, says Pyongyang is "effectively conducting slavery of its own people and for its own profit."

"This is just a terrible situation, and we know that it is not happening only at Yelabuga," he told DW. "We know there are construction workers in the occupied Ukrainian territories, North Koreans in lumber camps and, of course, tens of thousands of soldiers have been sent to fight — and die — on the front lines in Ukraine," Song added.

"Life in North Korea is not easy, but these people are being sent to Russia as slaves, with no freedom, and they are only allowed to keep a fraction of the money they earn," he said.

The challenge, he admits, is to find a way to halt this "trade in humanity."

How much can realistically be done?

"These countries share a border, so it is easy to transport workers, and no other agency can intervene," Song said. "Russia and China are both permanent members of the UN Security Council but are ignoring its resolutions on this issue. There is very little that can be done."

Song's rights organization is attempting to highlight the plight of North Korean workers and to create a "coalition of like-minded nations and agencies" to protect laborers — although he admits to being "pessimistic."

Pinkston shares those concerns, as well as fears over the emergence of a powerful bloc that appears to be "ripping up the post-World War II order on the rule of law and human rights" and is intent on taking a confrontational approach to other nations.

The weapons being manufactured at Yelabuga will assist in achieving those aims, he said.

"UN Security Council resolutions on North Korean workers, on weapons proliferation, on the sale of dual-use technologies are all being ignored, so I think we can say that the UN's sanctions regime is pretty much dead," Pinkston added.

North Korea developing its drone capabilities

It is clear that both Russia and Ukraine have gained important insights into the modern battlefield through their ongoing conflict, Pinkston said, with the emergence of drone technology arguably one of the most critical advances.

"And like everyone else, North Korea has been watching closely, 'learning-by-doing' and innovating its own drone capabilities," Pinkston said, adding that there are "serious implications" for the South Korean military as it also attempts to keep up its defensive capabilities against a new generation of drones in the North. 

To curb the deployment of North Korean laborers to Russia and the proliferation of weapons, the joint report calls on the US State Department to work with other countries to disrupt human trafficking networks and sanction those responsible.

It also urges the UN to work multilaterally to investigate the Yelabuga complex and to catalogue the abuses that have taken place. Moreover, it demands accountability for those who have carried out abuses and for victims to be protected.

The report adds that foreign companies that are operating as part of the Yelabuga special economic zone — there are "several" European companies and at least one US firm with a presence at the site — should be pressured to leave.

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

entries.title: New EU plan for Arctic warily eyes influence of Russia, US
entries.summary: The EU unveiled its priorities in the Arctic as it vies with Russia, China and the US for influence. EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage undermine Arctic security.
entries.content:
Europe

New EU plan for Arctic warily eyes influence of Russia, US

October 20, 2026

The EU unveiled its priorities in the Arctic as it vies with Russia, China and the US for influence. EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage undermine Arctic security.

The EU on Tuesday presented a new Arctic Strategy that outlines the bloc's priorities in the key region amid challenges such as security threats, climate change and mining. 

Russia is building up its military power in the Arctic, and US President Donald Trump has threatened Greenland, saying the Danish territory is needed for American security interests but later signed a deal with Denmark over US military access to the territory. China is also investing in the region and has shipping ambitions there.

The northern parts of Finland and Sweden, along with Greenland are located within the Arctic, meaning part of the region is in the European neighborhood.  Iceland and Norway, two other Arctic states, are also involved in the European single market.  

'Tectonic plates of geopolitics' colliding in Arctic

"The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

"When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned security in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture," she added.

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia "has reopened Soviet-era bases and is testing new weapons" in the Arctic.

"Drone incursions, GPS jamming and the sabotage of undersea cables undermine Arctic security," Kallas continued. Russia's shadow fleet, which is an attempt to circumvent Western sanctions, is active in the Arctic. 

On Arctic security, the EU plans to develop a maritime security hub in the region "to facilitate information sharing form seabed to space." The bloc also intends to expand European icebreaker capacity and extend its satellite surveillance program in the region.

However, the EU does not intend to compete with NATO in the region, EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela told DW. Twenty-three EU countries are members of NATO.

"NATO will remain basically the center of defense and the center of deterrence, but NATO doesn't have a budget, the member state has," Sikela said. "This is first about the proper focus and the proper use of resources of the NATO member states and about better coordination."

EU to boost climate research as Arctic faces ice melting crisis

In regard to the climate, the Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average. The melting of ice and glaciers in the Arctic pose risks to Europe such as prolonged heatwaves, drought and flooding. 

Sikela said, "Collaboration among the Arctic is very difficult," adding, "We're not getting information about the permafrost from the biggest part of the Arctic territory."

Sikela accused Russia of "unprecedented" actions in the Arctic and said the "catastrophic level of drilling and opening new mines" in the region is contributing to its rapid warming. The Arctic is rich in critical minerals and rare earth elements such as nickel.

As part of the EU Arctic Strategy, the bloc intends "to strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring" and launch flagship projects utilizing AI to "anticipate extreme weather and cascading disasters such as coastal flooding."

Although Russia and other non-EU countries such as Norway drill in the Arctic, the EU does not want to expand new drilling in the region. European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said the EU's view "on drilling in the Arctic remains the same and it's very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground."  

Greenland submarine cable route project bypasses US

Regarding economic interests in the Arctic, the bloc may take further steps to bypass the US. The strategy calls for "resilient submarine cable connectivity linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions towards Canada and Japan."

The EU also outlined new plans regarding the residents of the Arctic region. The bloc wants to strengthen dialogue with Indigenous people along with expanding Erasmus+ opportunities for Arctic youth.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: France plans 'massive' weekend police surge amid protests
entries.summary: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told parliament the government would respond and reinforce police in major cities. He also accused extreme-left groups of trying to hijack what began as protests. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published October 19, 2026last updated October 20, 2026

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told parliament the government would respond and reinforce police in major cities. He also accused extreme-left groups of trying to hijack what began as protests. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said adequate support for police was essential, both to allow public protests and to keep the peace
  • He accused 'ultra-left and extreme left' groups of planning to escalate and politicize the unrest as part of an 'insurrectionary plan'
  • France was rocked over the weekend by some of its worst rioting in recent years over amid anti-government protests
  • Curfews on Monday night helped restore calm, Lecornu said, with more planned as necessary going forward
  • Italy's Meloni considers curfew, tougher youth detention rules, after Milan riots
  • Albania's PM says 'red line' was crossed during anti-government demos and clashes

Follow below for the latest on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on Tuesday, October 20:  

Skip next section Italy to send military to Milan

Italy to send military to Milan

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said 500 troops would be sent to the city of Milan until January. They will help police after violent clashes in the city over the weekend.

Meloni said a Cabinet meeting also approved measures to make the detention of minors easier, to impose fines on their parents for any damage and to introduce the crime of "violent participation in a demonstration."

"Protesting is a right, devastating our cities is not," Meloni said in a video on X.

Skip next section What restrictions on gatherings are in place in major cities besides Paris?

What restrictions on gatherings are in place in major cities besides Paris?

At least four other cities — Lyon, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille — have announced continued localized restrictions that will take effect on Tuesday night.

In Lyon, the prefect of the Rhone region, ordered another curfew from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. in what's known colloquially as the hypercentre of the old city — an area spanning the first and second Arondissements and other key historic zones like the city hall, the Place Bellecour pedestrian square and the commercial and historic neighborhood Les Cordeliers.

Prefect Etienne Guyot also said a ban on what French authorities term attroupements — gatherings of people deemed to have the potential to threaten public order — from 4 p.m. until 9 p.m. would also apply.

In Bordeaux, unaccompanied minors will not be allowed on the streets from 10 p.m. until 7 a.m. "in the sectors particularly affected by the pillages of October 17," Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas said.

She said this was aimed to "prevent all new attacks on businesses" in a series of key central streets and squares. The restrictions were set to apply until next Monday, October 26.

And to the south in Nice, the city center sector, the old city and the Trachel-Gare du Sud sectors will be restricted from 9 p.m. until 6 a.m. until Sunday, October 25.

Authorities in Marseille, France's second-largest city, announced a nightly curfew for unaccompanied minors from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. through Friday in central shopping streets and sensitive areas.

Skip next section Paris police announces overnight curfew in heart of city center

Paris police announces overnight curfew in heart of city center

Paris police said on Tuesday evening that a curfew would be in effect from 11 p.m. local time until 6 a.m. in the heart of the city center in the 1st arrondissement district, known as des Halles, and at the Place de la Republique.

The 1st arrondissement is home to the Louvre Museum, the Arc de Triomphe, and Paris' famous commercial shopping street the Rue de Rivoli, among other landmarks near the banks of the River Seine.

Beyond this, police also announced a ban on protesting — but not a full curfew — in a series of areas in the capital. The same parts of the city would be affected as was the case with the broader restrictions of Monday night, the prefecture said.

Skip next section France's Lecornu accuses 'far-left' of 'insurrectionary plan' to escalate protests

France's Lecornu accuses 'far-left' of 'insurrectionary plan' to escalate protests

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has told French lawmakers that authorities would mobilize a "massive" security presence next weekend, after organizers announced plans for new protests. 

"The deployment for next Saturday will be massive," Lecornu said in the National Assembly.

He said the security operation last weekend had been "too static and not mobile enough."

Lecornu said adequate support for security forces was "the precondition for everything" when trying to both allow peaceful protests but also keep order, saying that "1,000 injured police and gendarmes over the weekend" nationwide was unacceptable.

Lecornu said the national public message in response should convey to them "clear, frank and massive support."

The prime minister also accused what he referred to as small ultra-left and extreme-left groups in certain locations of forging an "insurrectionary plan" that fueled the violent rioting over the weekend for which the government could provide evidence.

"What happened at the mayoral office of Limoges was an example. You have a first arrest that was carried out this morning," Lecornu said. "This individual arrested is, unfortunately, already known to [security] services."

He said authorities would not tolerate such groups "marching on the Elysee or Matignon," referring to the offices and residences of President Emmanuel Macron and himself as head of government, and saying that some of these groups had harbored such ambitions.

Skip next section Paris police set up reporting platform for violence, damage, looting

Paris police set up reporting platform for violence, damage, looting

The Paris police prefecture has launched an online portal inviting people to upload evidence of criminal unrest over the weekend.

"Withness to violence, damage, or looting in recent days? The [Paris police prefecture] has decided to create a dedicated platform," it wrote online.

It urged people who thought they might have relevant information not to delay.

"Send all your images to the police services to help them quickly identify and apprehend the perpetrators," police said.

Skip next section Italy plans to facilitate detention of minors in response to unrest

Italy plans to facilitate detention of minors in response to unrest

Italy will approve new security measures targeting minors on Tuesday, government politicians said, after days of unrest in several cities, but particularly in Milan. 

Under the planned rules, authorities will be authorized to detain people under the age of 18 for up to 12 hours, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a threat, Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini said.

"We want to intervene quickly on young people," Salvini told the RTL radio broadcaster ahead of a meeting of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's Cabinet called on Tuesday to approve the measures. 

Rome is also expected to deploy an additional 500 army troops in Milan as authorities fear more widespread unrest at demonstrations planned for Saturday.

The French student and youth protests first showed signs of spilling into Italy on Friday, with initially peaceful events coinciding with the pre-existing anti-government protest magnet known as "No Meloni Day."

The unrest persisted and intensified heading into the weekend as several hundred hooded individuals, many of them thought to be minors, set fires and looted shops in the centers of Milan and other cities.

Meloni has passed a steady stream of security and law-and-order crackdowns since taking office in 2022, visible among other places in the prison population increasing by almost one-fifth, or around 10,000 people, over four years.

Skip next section French police arrest man over Limoges town hall fire

French police arrest man over Limoges town hall fire

French authorities have arrested a 40-year-old man in connection with the fire that destroyed the historic Limoges town hall during unrest over the weekend.

The building, dating from 1883, was engulfed by fire on Saturday. Its roof and belfry collapsed, making the building's destruction a symbol of the violence that accompanied nationwide protests.

The suspect was arrested by RAID, France's elite police unit, near Limoges. Prosecutors say he had previously been flagged as a potential security threat.

France's Counter-Terrorism Sub-Directorate has joined the investigation, while Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin says anti-terror prosecutors will decide whether to classify the case as a terrorist act.

Skip next section Dott, Lime count losses after Paris protesters burn shared e-Bikes

Dott, Lime count losses after Paris protesters burn shared e-Bikes

In Paris, sights of e-bikes thrown into burning piles became a common sight over the weekend, prompting bike makers Dott and Lime to asses their losses.

Shared mobility operator Dott, in a statement to Reuters on Monday, said that about 300 of its electric bikes were destroyed and 120 severely damaged in Paris, during the nationwide anti-government protests on Saturday. The company has about 6,000 bikes int he city.

Dott also said 80 vehicles, including bikes and scooters were destroyed in Bordeux and another 30-40 Scooters in Lyon. It estimates the damage at about €400,000 ($450,000).

Lime, another entity for shared electric bikes, said 6% of its Paris fleet was destroyed or damaged.

Ahead of demonstrations, Lime said it worked with the police to remove vehicles from designated protest routes and restricted parking or riding in high-risk areas.

Smovengo, operator ​of the Vélib' Métropole bike-sharing service in Paris, told Reuters that some 300 of its 20,000 bike fleet were damaged or stolen over the weekend.

E-bikes often use lithium-ion batteries that can ignite and produce intense fires and toxic smoke.

There was no indication that e-bike operators were specifically targeted during the protests. Rather, their ready availability likely played a role as protesters used them to build barricades or build fires.

Skip next section France to impose 'targeted curfews' wherever necessary, says PM

France to impose 'targeted curfews' wherever necessary, says PM

Francewill impose new curfews in areas where they are required, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said Tuesday after the first night of partial curfews in major cities including Paris.

Lecornu said the targeted curfews had helped keep the peace overnight after a turbulent weekend that saw protesters take aim at state institutions.

"Targeted curfews have contributed to calm overnight," the premier wrote on X. "Tonight new curfews will be decided where the situation requires it. These decisions will be made on the ground, by the prefects, in coordination with the Mayors," he said.

Police confirmed the night had passed without major incidents across France.

Skip next section Trump blames immigrants, Muslims, for French unrest in attack on Democrats

Trump blames immigrants, Muslims, for French unrest in attack on Democrats

US President Donald Trump on Monday cited the unrest in France as an example while warning of what he alleged could happen in the United States if opposition Democrats were in power, without providing evidence to support the claim.

At a rally supporting the Republican Senate candidate in Kansas, Trump described France as a formerly great nation that had been "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists."

"When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what ​the radical Dumocrats want to do to America," he said, using the altered version of his opponents' name that he often employs as an insult.

Ahead of the rally, Trump told reporters at the White House that he had warned French President Emmanuel Macron he was "making a big mistake."

"The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn't the deal," he said, adding: "We closed our borders. He didn't."

The US president's return to his signature anti-immigration, anti-Muslim rhetoric, which he used to some effect in his election campaigns, comes as his party seeks to avoid a drubbing in the November midterm elections.

His comments echo previous remarks by Republican colleagues. Vice President JD Vance, for example, argued that the French protests occurred because "Western liberals imported the third world into France."

Skip next section A turbulent weekend in France: How did it come to be?

A turbulent weekend in France: How did it come to be?

Catherine Field, a journalist in Paris, told DW why demonstrations were different this time. Protests markedly sprang up in different parts of the capital city and elsewhere, particularly taking aim at state institutions. Police appeared to have lost some sense of control, she said. Listen to the full conversation here:

Skip next section READ: What has the French government said about the rioting in France?

READ: What has the French government said about the rioting in France?

French President Emmanuel Macron has vowed to punish those responsible for the rioting and violence over the weekend.

He also acknowledged "failures in anticipation and intelligence" by police and sought to make clear the distinction between rioters and demonstrators.

Skip next section Are there more protests planned in France?

Are there more protests planned in France?

The answer is yes. French unions have called for a new round of rallies on November 5.

Earlier on Monday, French President Emmanuel Macron blamed organized ultraleft groups for the rioting and looting on Saturday.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday that he was "fully resolved to restore public order."

He called for imposing localized curfews, as is in place overnight into Tuesday (see below), but said there was "no question" of imposing a full curfew on entire cities.

But Lecornu refused to rule out declaring a state of emergency, which would give authorities sweeping powers to restrict public gatherings.

Skip next section Where are curfews in place in France?

Where are curfews in place in France?

Authorities in France have announced localized curfews in several areas including:

  • In northern France, including Lille, Douai, Denain and Wattignies, a curfew for minors is in place for the next two days from 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) to 6 a.m.
  • In the south, including Nice, where a specific curfew is in place for minors in the city center.
  • Two areas in Paris, where curfew prohibits anyone from entering or remaining on the Place de la République, where rioting took place Saturday, and the shopping neighborhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.
  • The partial curfew in Paris went into effect at 11 p.m. Monday and remains in place until 6 a.m. Tuesday.

Skip next section Foreign governments issue France travel warnings

Foreign governments issue France travel warnings

Several countries around the world, including China, Malaysia, Germany and the United States, have advised citizens traveling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution in the wake of large-scale protests and looting in major cities.

China's Foreign Ministry urged Chinese nationals in France to remain alert to potential risks, increase safety precautions, and avoid ​areas where demonstrations are taking place.

Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that, while ⁠travel to France remains unrestricted, ​Malaysians are advised to consider postponing non-essential trips until the situation improves.

The Malaysian embassy in Paris has issued an advisory urging citizens already in France to exercise caution and remain vigilant.

The US State Department issued an alert on Monday warning Americans to avoid demonstrations in major French cities, while an alert issued by the American embassy in Paris noted new curfews ordered in cities including Paris and Lille.

"Avoid the areas of the demonstrations," the warning said.

And in Europe, some of France's direct neighbors have also issued travel advice to citizens.

The German Foreign Ministry said ‌further riots couldn't be ruled out and urged German nationals to follow instructions from local police. It warned citizens that they could face fines if they fail to adhere to requests to leave unauthorized demonstrations.

Governments in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Poland, Denmark, Sweden, ​Finland and Norway also issued warnings to avoid protests.

entries.title: Germany news: Hackers release AfD party emails
entries.summary: Germany's far-right AfD has launched an inquiry after the release of thousands of emails following a cyberattack. Also, investors pledged billions for Germany at a major summit in Berlin. DW has more news from Germany.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Hackers release AfD party emails

Published October 20, 2026last updated October 20, 2026

Germany's far-right AfD has launched an inquiry after the release of thousands of emails following a cyberattack. Also, investors pledged billions for Germany at a major summit in Berlin. DW has more news from Germany.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Messages of some 281 gigabytes of data were released under the headline "The party's own records, unedited'
  • The Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin has produced commitments to the tune of billions, officials say
  • Under an agreement announced at the summit, Germany is to enhance cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) with US company Nvidia
  • Entry-level jobs involving routine tasks often left to AI are still vital for young people to learn basic skills, according to Siemens
  • Berlin's Left Party, which has been accused of antisemitism, is debating the future of a member who has come under fire for anti-Israel stances

This is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 20, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section WATCH — Inside the huge AfD email leak rocking German politics

WATCH — Inside the huge AfD email leak rocking German politics

More than 421,000 emails linked to Germany's far-right AfD have been published following a cyberattack (see additional entry below).

The alleged material includes private communications, sensitive personal data and reported references to racism, antisemitism and Nazi ideology, although much of the trove has not yet been independently verified.

Could this become one of the biggest political data leaks in modern German history?

Skip next section Supermarket goes viral after reply to racist comment

Supermarket goes viral after reply to racist comment

A German supermarket is getting attention online after responding to a customer who objected to its diverse workforce.

Skip next section Pro-Palestinian protesters glue themselves in front of Berlin Rheinmetall facility

Pro-Palestinian protesters glue themselves in front of Berlin Rheinmetall facility

Nine pro-Palestinian protesters seeking an end to Western arms exports to Israel glued themselves to the ground in front of a Berlin facility belonging to German weapons manufacturer Rheinmetall.

Berlin police responded to the incident at 5:30 a.m. (0330 UTC) with 11 protesters at the site. The "Peacefully Against Genocide" group was behind the action.

The factory began arms production in June. It is involved in the production of shell casings for artillery ammunition and parts for kamikaze drones, according to local public broadcaster RBB. 

It is unclear how much the facility in Berlin's Wedding neighborhood is involved with weapons for Israel. Rheinmetall, however, is Germany's largest arms manufacturer.

In the western German state of Hesse, seven people also blocked the entry to the Rheinmetall facility in the city of Kassel, according to local police.

In addition, demonstrators against weapons exports glued themselves in front of a weapons company in the western city of Kaiserslautern.

Skip next section Far-right AfD says emails stolen in September cyberattack

Far-right AfD says emails stolen in September cyberattack

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) said on Tuesday that it was looking into the theft and subsequent online publication of emails stolen by unidentified hackers during a cyberattack last month.

An AfD spokesperson said the hackers had targeted a hosting provider used by the party and appeared to have copied data from a small number of mostly inactive email accounts.

"The recent online publication of what is presumably a portion of this data is currently being investigated," the spokesperson said. "A preliminary assessment can only be provided once this investigation has been concluded."

Although the spokesperson did not say how much data was stolen, an earlier report by the mass-circulation daily Bild put the number of AfD-linked emails published at more than 420,000.

According to Bild, the material published included not only emails sent by party figures such as co-leader Alice Weidel but also bank statements, academic certificates and membership lists.

The website hosting the material was offline by Tuesday afternoon.

However, archived versions showed a volume of 281 gigabytes of data under the headline "The party's own records, unedited."

The emails and other materials published have not yet been certified as authentic by any independent body.

The AfD, several state chapters of which have been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by regional branches of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, has been topping recent national opinion polls and made gains in recent state elections.

Some politicians and civil society groups have called for it to be banned, arguing that the party is a threat to democracy, an accusation the party has rejected.

Skip next section In depth: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand

In depth: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand

While Berlin hosts a summit on investment in Germany, an increasing amount of US capital is flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses.

As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

Read all the details here: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand

Skip next section High energy prices weigh on German economic confidence

High energy prices weigh on German economic confidence

German economic confidence — like that across the eurozone in general — deteriorated in October, according to experts at the Mannheim-based Center for European Economic Research (ZEW).

The ZEW's monthly economic confidence index fell to a three-month low on Tuesday, down to 28.1 from 34.7 in September. That is nearly two points lower than forecast.

"Private consumption and investment remain weak because of high energy prices: They put real incomes under pressure, increase production costs and keep inflation higher for longer," said ZEW President Achim Wambach.

"The German economy," added Wambach, "is slowly emerging from stagnation, but the recovery is not self-sustaining."

The biggest losers in this latest index were banks, insurers, the service sector and the telecommunications industry.

Winners were seen in the metal manufacturing and electronics industries.

ZEW compiles its monthly surveys from interviews with banking, insurance and financial industry experts and businesses on their expectations for economic and capital market developments.

The ZEW's index is considered a key indicator for Germany's economic development.

Tuesday's survey was based on interviews with 178 analysts between October 12 and 19, 2026.

Skip next section Merz vaunts Germans' 'predictable' character in search of investments

Merz vaunts Germans' 'predictable' character in search of investments

Chancellor Friedrich Merzhas indulged in an abundance of the most common cliches about his country and compatriots while trying to portray Germany as the ideal place to do business at an investment summit.

"Germans are hardworking, going to bed early, rising before dawn," he told the domestic and international guests at the Invest in Germany Summit.

"Worst traffic is in the morning between 6 and 7," he said.

"On holidays, we are first on the beach, spreading towels before breakfast. If we agree on delivery dates, we stick to it. If you invite friends from Germany for dinner at 7, we will arrive at 6:58.

"We are reliable, predictable, precise, and unsurprising," the chancellor continued. "We are, in short, what investors like most."

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil also used blunt humor in his appeal to potential investors, saying in his speech simply: "I want your money."

Both pitches appear to have succeeded, with investment commitments worth billions made at the summit.

Skip next section More than €225 billion investment committed at summit — economy minister

More than €225 billion investment committed at summit — economy minister

More than €225 billion ($252.5 billion) has so far been pledged in investments in Germany at a summit in Berlin attended by top business leaders, German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said on Tuesday.

Reiche did not give any details about the commitments made so far, but told broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that the figure only included deals above a volume of €100 million.

Among those planning to invest in Europe's largest economy is online retail giant Amazon, which said it intended to pour some €16 billion into Germany next year for various schemes.

The company said these would include "the expansion of data centers and AI infrastructure, high-speed satellite internet through Amazon Leo, new logistics projects across the country, and a major new production slate by Prime Video."

"Germany is a hub of innovation and one of the most attractive investment opportunities in Europe," David Zapolsky, Amazon's chief global affairs and legal officer, was quoted as saying in a statement.

"That is why we have invested more than €100 billion here since 2010, and why we plan to invest an additional €16 billion in 2027. We want German businesses, communities, and creators to have the infrastructure and tools they need to compete and grow."

More than 200 German and international executives from large corporations, investment banks and funds are attending the gathering, entitled the Invest in Germany Summit.

Skip next section Left Party debates measures on Israel-critical state parliamentarian

Left Party debates measures on Israel-critical state parliamentarian

The Left Party in Berlin, which has faced accusations of being antisemitic, is holding a meeting to discuss how to deal with its parliamentarian Vanessa Emde, who has raised controversy with pro-Palestinian statements.

Among other things, Emde has supported the idea that there is no right to exist for states, but only for people — thus seemingly going against Germany's firm support of Israel's right to existence.

Emde has refused to retract any of her statements.

She has also criticized a statement on antisemitism that she had signed along with all other members of the Left's parliamentary party in which the signatories committed to upholding Israel's right to existence.

Emde is to attend the online meeting.

Greens, SPD agree to coalition negotiations

This comes as both the Berlin Green Party and the Social Democrats (SPD) confirmed that they were ready to begin coalition negotiations with the Left Party on forming a joint government in the city-state.

The Left Party is due to decide on the issue on October 31 at a party conference.

The three parties held preliminary discussions on the accusations of antisemitism and links to organized crime leveled at the Left Party before beginning the exploratory talks that precede final coalition negotiations.

The Left Party emerged from September 20 elections in Berlin as the strongest party with 25.7% of the vote.

Both the Greens (14.3%) and the center-left SPD (12.1%) came in behind the conservative Christian Democrats (18.8%), who led a previous coalition in Berlin with the SPD.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) received 16.3% of the vote, but so far, all other parties are officially refusing to enter into any form of cooperation with it at either federal or state level. 

Skip next section AI cooperation with US' Nvidia announced as investment summit continues

AI cooperation with US' Nvidia announced as investment summit continues

The Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin entered its second and final day on Tuesday after opening the previous evening with a speech by Chancellor Friedrich Merz that included the words: "Germany is open for business."

The summit has already yielded an agreement to deepen cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) in German industry between Germany and US tech giant Nvidia.

Merz and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the combination of Germany's engineering expertise and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy over the long term.

More than 200 German and international executives representing large corporations, investment banks and funds are attending the event, with closed-door talks scheduled for Tuesday.

The summit aims to attract foreign investment to Germany. Organizers highlight the country's sound public finances, triple-A credit rating as the only G7 nation to hold one, strong rule of law and leading position in European patent filings.

Despite these advantages, Germany has struggled to attract foreign investment in recent years, with high energy prices and labor costs acting as deterrents.

Government sources say investment will be vital to help bridge gaps in public funding as the country seeks to improve infrastructure and support companies' transition to climate-neutral production.

The summit is also being attended by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, who also serves as Merz's deputy.

Skip next section Protesters glue themselves to road outside Rheinmetall plant

Protesters glue themselves to road outside Rheinmetall plant

Nine protesters have glued themselves to the road outside a plant run by defense contractor Rheinmetall in Berlin's Wedding district, police said on Tuesday.

Officers have been trying since the early morning to detach the group, a police spokeswoman said.

She said as many as 90 officers had been deployed to the site, where altogether 11 protesters were gathered.

Rheinmetall is Germany's largest weapons manufacturer.

The plant in Wedding, where production began earlier this year, has been the target of several protests, with climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg among those participating.

Skip next section Young workers need to develop skills away from AI — Siemens

Young workers need to develop skills away from AI — Siemens

German industrial giant Siemens has warned against eliminating entry-level jobs that are now increasingly left to artificial intelligence (AI), saying young workers could be left without essential skills, including those needed to monitor AI-generated work.

Judith Wiese, the company's chief people and sustainability officer, said that handing certain routine tasks to AI meant that young employees would not gain hands-on experience that could benefit them later in their careers.

Wiese said it was necessary, for example, for software developers to be able to write their own code so they could critically examine the code produced by AI.

"The crucial question is always: What do I need to have done, checked and seen myself to avoid being misled by AI?" she said.

However, Wiese said AI could also help employees acquire skills more quickly, while older colleagues could learn from younger ones who had grown up using AI.

Wiese said it was still too early to say how AI would impact employment.

Noting that Siemens has some 30,000 software engineers, she said: "You can use the additional productivity either to do the same work with fewer people or to do more with the same number of employees."

Wiese also pointed out that AI was speeding up work processes, enabling the exploration of new ideas and creating projects that would not have been possible without it.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

DW''s newsroom in Bonn bids a warm guten Tag to all its readers as a previously balmy October decides to move toward more wintry chill.

As Chancellor Merz hosts an investment conference in Berlin where developments in AI is taking center stage, industrial giant Siemens has warned that the technology does not only bring advantages.

The controversy over alleged antisemitism in Berlin's Left Party, which might well soon lead a leftist coalition in the city-state, continues, with the party itself debating what to do about a member who has expressed strong anti-Israel views.

And people in Germany are likely to face much longer waits for doctors' appointments from next year, according to an organization managing family doctors and therapists across Germany.

Read on here for more on these and other stories with a German slant.

entries.title: Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro tied ahead of runoff vote
entries.summary: With just under a week to go before the decisive presidential runoff election, polls show left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro are virtually tied.
entries.content:
Brazil

Brazil's Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro tied ahead of runoff vote

October 20, 2026

With just under a week to go before the decisive presidential runoff election, polls show left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro are virtually tied.

There are only a few days left until Brazil's runoff election on October 25, with neither left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva nor right-wing populist Flavio Bolsonaro a clear favorite.

While three polls from last week showed a razor-thin lead for Bolsonaro, the PoderData polling institute has now projected 50% voter backing for each candidate.

This election could end up as close as the one held in 2022, when Lula narrowly beat Flavio Bolsonaro's father, Jair Messias Bolsonaro, with just 50.9% of the vote. Jair Bolsonaro, incidentally, was later jailed for attempting a coup to hold onto power.

His son, Flavio, surprisingly won the first round of voting on October 4 by securing 47% of the vote. Bolsonaro's right-wing bloc also won many additional seats in Congress, primarily at the expense of Brazil's centrist parties. And in the week following the first round of voting, polls showed Bolsonaro commanding a lead of up to six percentage points.

Yet last week, Lula managed to gain momentum through nationwide mass rallies and his dynamic social media presence. Bolsonaro, in contrast, had scaled back street campaigning in light of his strong poll numbers.

That turned out to be a mistake. Now he, too, is once more mobilizing supporters to stage major rallies across Brazil as the country readies for the runoff.

A polarized nation

The rivalry between Lula's left-wing camp and Bolsonaro's far-right bloc has shaped Brazilian politics for the past decade.

Jair Bolsonaro gained nationwide recognition during the 2016 impeachment proceedings against Lula's political protegee, then-President Dilma Rousseff. He went on to win the 2018 presidential election while Lula was serving a prison sentence on corruption charges.

But when Lula's conviction was overturned, the former trade union leader staged a political comeback in 2022.

This polarization is responsible for the disappearance of centrist parties and a political alternative, or "third way," said political scientist Marco Aurelio Nogueira.

"The divide between Lula and Bolsonarism has paralyzed Brazilian politics, and anything that didn't belong to one pole or the other has disappeared," Nogueira told DW. This polarization is fueled by social media, the expert added, saying that "platforms' algorithms thrive on conflict and reward excitement."

Flavio Bolsonaro a toned-down version of his father

Nogueira said Flavio Bolsonaro's calm demeanor could explain why he has a realistic chance of defeating Lula, unlike his father in 2022.

"Jair Messias Bolsonaro was a crude, rhetorically aggressive figure," said Nogueira. "Flavio Bolsonaro, on the other hand, casts himself as more moderate and gives Bolsonarism a more youthful image. He communicates skillfully, posts well-produced videos, and addresses workers' issues, such as the introduction of the five-day workweek."

Lula's recent promise to shorten workweek hours has lent momentum to his campaign. Alarmed by Lula's rising poll numbers, Bolsonaro gave up his opposition to the move and voted in favor of the five-day workweek.

Bolsonaro is now taking a less radical stance on fiscal policy, too. Although he had announced drastic budget cuts before the first round of voting, modeled on the policies of his libertarian Argentine ally Javier Milei, he now intends to continue Lula's social programs. That said, Bolsonaro has not presented a plan for how he intends to reduce Brazil's high public debt.

Banco Master corruption scandal shapes race

The election campaign has been overshadowed by a massive corruption scandal surrounding the insolvent financial institution Banco Master. Daniel Vorcaro, the bank's former owner, is under investigation for fraud, money laundering and corruption.

Vorcaro is accused of having bribed decision-makers in the world of politics, finance and the judiciary. Several Supreme Court justices are said to be involved in the scandal, which involved dubious sex parties and millions in reported payouts. Judges from both the Lula camp and some appointed by Jair Bolsonaro are said to be tied up in the scandal.

Flavio Bolsonaro is alleged to have accepted goods and services from Vorcaro, including a €10 million donation for a film about his father's life. Yet Lula has not been able to capitalize on his rival's alleged failings. After all, his very own son is implicated in another corruption scandal. Moreover, Bolsonaro has repeatedly drawn attention to Lula's 2017 conviction for corruption, even though it was later overturned by the Supreme Court.

Friday's debate key to reaching voters

Political scientist Nogueira believes the mudslinging between both candidates over who is more corrupt has left voters jaded.

"There are constant reports about scandals and mutual accusations from all sides," said Nogueira. "As a result, the effect is essentially canceled out in the election campaign. The average voter tunes out and no longer attaches much importance to these accusations when making a voting decision."

Both candidates held their first live television debate on Sunday. On Friday, two days before the runoff election, they will face off once more on Brazil's largest broadcaster, Globo. The debate will likely have a significant influence on the October 25 vote.

Experts believe the key for both candidates will be to not be rattled by provocations from the other side. Concrete policies, in turn, will only play a minor role in the debate.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Who are the women powering India's youth-led 'Cockroach' protests?
entries.summary: Facing online harassment and police detentions, women are taking to the streets of Indian cities in large numbers for the youth-led "Cockroach" protests. Amid a large-scale crackdown, they refuse to be seen as victims.
entries.content:
India

Who are the women powering India's youth-led 'Cockroach' protests?

October 20, 2026

Facing online harassment and police detentions, women are taking to the streets of Indian cities in large numbers for the youth-led "Cockroach" protests. Amid a large-scale crackdown, they refuse to be seen as victims.

On July 20, Navkiran Natt and her partner set out for the magistrate's office in New Delhi to get married. They arrived to find a tense situation, with police gathering to break up a youth-led march on Parliament. Office staff — and the couple's wedding witnesses — were running late due to barricades.

The protest movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) had announced the march to demand the resignation of India's then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. 

The protesters were met with heavy resistance from security forces, who had deployed batons, tear gas and pellet-firing shotguns, leading to injuries and mass detentions.

Less than three months later, on October 10, Natt left home early in the morning and spent the day crisscrossing the locked-down Indian capital looking for a protest she could join. 

"The success of this protest is not how many people will reach Jantar Mantar," she told DW, referring to the protest site in central New Delhi. "It's that even after all this barricading and state violence, people are leaving their homes to join."

What are these protests about?

The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). 

After succeeding in seeing Pradhan step down in late July, the CJP is now demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were removed from draft electoral rolls nationwide.

With CJP leadership in judicial custody or under threat of detention, one name has fast become synonymous with the demonstrations: student leader Neha Bora, who prefers to use the pronoun they/them. 

Bora has run through the streets to dodge police officials, climbed barricades in the face of security personnel, shouted slogans from detention vans and addressed press conferences alongside CJP spokespersons and others.

They are the president of the All India Students' Association, the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) Liberation (CPI-ML).

"In extremely disappointing, fearful, tyrannical times, people try to gather hope from whatever source they can … If these people are fighting, then probably we can also fight," Bora told DW.

"It is a responsibility that you owe to people," they added.

Women out on the streets in large numbers

The Cockroach-led demonstrations also come at a time when women and members of the LGBTQ+ community are calling for greater autonomy for women in the aftermath of the gang rape of a 17-year-old girl in New Delhi in late September, placing the issue of safety in India back into the spotlight.

According to the National Crime Records Bureau, 441,534 cases of crimes against women were registered in 2024, averaging 1,210 cases per day. Experts say these official statistics can only give a partial account of gendered violence. 

But despite facing sexualized backlash from police on the streets and from online mobs, the women and genderqueer people leading the movement reject being cast as victims.

"The "beti bachao" [save the daughter] thing just doesn't cut it with this generation. It is a very specific ask: see us as political beings, free beings," activist Kavita Krishnan told DW.

"Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao" (Save the Daughter, Educate the Daughter) is a flagship BJP government program launched in 2015.

Protest as daily life

These days, Gurmehar Kaur's day starts like any other — a workout or a yoga class — and often ends with Indian Youth Congress' lawyers getting her released from police detention.

"Resistance can't be a separate event … a big day, and then you go back to your regular life," she told DW.

The 29-year-old author of "The Young and the Restless: Youth and Politics in India" spent a better part of the last decade in the public eye.

This year, she joined the youth wing of India's main opposition party, The Congress, whose offices are located a stone's throw away from Jantar Mantar, the hub of the last wave of protests.

Kaur said her political association has given her access to resources that can support the movement, offering a safety net for protesters "regardless of their political affiliation."

At a time when authorities are cracking down on CJP protesters, she said opposition members like her have a duty to fulfill: "Show up, put your body on the line."

Price of visibility

But showing up often comes with a cost, especially for women and queer protesters.

Kaur explained how male colleagues often "feel quite elated when their photos are in the media." However, for her, "attention is equal to death and rape threats and humiliation and abuse."

Navkiran Natt, an activist most significantly associated with the 2020–2021 farmers' protests, echoes Kaur's experience.

"If a woman is leading the protest, the first attack is on her sexuality," she said.

Social media images have shown women protesters with their clothes torn during clashes with police.

Delhi officials have denied allegations of manhandling, adding that women protesters were treated with "dignity."

Student leader Bora refuted the police's claim, saying that a small number of female personnel were available to handle a large number of female protesters.

"Several women protesters came to protect me and prevent me from getting detained," they said.

Authorities have registered a police case against a journalist who accused a senior Delhi police officer of sexual harassment under an Indian law meant to prevent crimes against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. They say her own allegations are under investigation.

The internet was also flooded with AI-made, sexualized images of women protesters edited into protest photos.

Why activists say the tactic is failing

This has not prevented protesters from taking to the streets even the day after being detained by authorities.

"They don't know what they're dealing with," activist Krishnan said, referring to the government's crackdown on demonstrators.

She said authorities assume sexual humiliation will scare women off, but "this is not a generation that thinks of… sexual violence as being something shameful."

She was at the forefront of demonstrations after the 2012 "Nirbhaya" gang rape, where slogans like "Hang the rapists" were seen in public. This time, however, she said the anger "is not going to be about masculine displays of honor."

It is about "dignity and freedom ... Women face all kinds of problems in every country, and Indian women are no different," she added.

Krishnan said the youth-led protests are part of a wider global wave of "civilizational, cultural nationalism," which uses gender and the language of protection, whether of daughters, families or tradition, to rally support against minorities, immigrants and trans people.

"You listen to the rhetoric of Donald Trump or Viktor Orban or the Alternative for Germany (AfD). It is the same," she said, referring to politics in the United States and Europe. "If you look at what's happening in India, you may be able to better understand what's happening in your country."

These young Indians, she said, are refusing to be taken in. They are "fighting back for a language of the future, a language that has hope."
